{{Short description|American nuclear physicist (1921–1997)}}
[[File:Albert L. Latter, 1964.jpg|alt=Photo of Latter in 1964|thumb|Latter in 1964]]
'''Albert Louis Latter''' (October 17, 1921, [[Kokomo, Indiana]] – June 8, 1997, [[Pacific Palisades, Los Angeles]]) was an American nuclear physicist and leading expert on nuclear weapons.<ref name=NYTimes>{{cite news|title=Obituary. Albert L. Latter, 76, Physicist and Expert on Nuclear Arms|newspaper=New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/06/27/us/albert-l-latter-76-physicist-and-expert-on-nuclear-arms.html|author=Pace, Eric|date=June 27, 1997|page=6, Section B}}</ref>

==Biography==
Latter graduated from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) with a bachelor's degree in mathematics and physics in 1941 and with a Ph.D. in physics in 1951.<ref name=NYTimes/> Immediately after receiving his Ph.D. he joined the [[Santa Monica]] headquarters of [[RAND Corporation]], where for the next twenty years he worked on nuclear weapons.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.882112|title=Obituary. Albert Louis Latter|year=1998|last1=Brode|first1=Harold L.|author-link=Harold L. Brode|journal=Physics Today|volume=51|pages=75–76|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In the 1950s Albert Latter and [[Edward Teller]] worked together on the [[United States Air Force Scientific Advisory Board]],<ref name=NYTimes/> where Teller attended his first meeting as a member in early 1952 at the invitation of his old friend [[Theodore von Karman]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Goodchild, Peter|author-link=Peter Goodchild|title=Edward Teller, the Real Dr. Strangelove|publisher=Harvard University Press|year=2004|page=193|isbn=9780674016699 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VSrCXJrjjzMC&pg=PA193}}</ref> Teller and Latter were the co-authors of the controversial book ''Our Nuclear Future: Facts, Dangers, and Opportunities'', published in 1958 by Criterion Books.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1126/science.127.3305.1042.b|title=Review of ''Our Nuclear Future: Facts, Dangers and Opportunities'' by Edward Teller and Albert L. Latter|year=1958|last1=Selove|first1=Walter|journal=Science|volume=127|issue=3305|page=1042|s2cid=239881549}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.3062706|title=Review of ''Our Nuclear Future'' by Edward Teller and Albert L. Latter|year=1958|last=Dyson|first=Freeman J.|author-link=Freeman Dyson|journal=Physics Today|volume=11|issue=8|pages=38–40|bibcode=1958PhT....11h..38T}}</ref>

{{blockquote|An American delegate to the 1959 nuclear test ban negotiations in Geneva, Latter studied seismic detection, which helped lead to the U.S. approval of the Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963.<br />He was the first American scientist to theorize that high-yield nuclear devices will emit a large fraction of their energy as high temperature X-rays, a discovery that demonstrated the vulnerability of offensive and defensive strategic missiles.<ref name=LATimes>{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-06-27-mn-7355-story.html|title=Obituary. Albert Latter; Physicist, Nuclear Weapons Expert|author=Oliver, Myrna|date=June 27, 1997|newspaper=L. A. Times}}</ref>}}

{{blockquote|In 1960, Dr. Latter became head of the physics department at Rand, where the aspects of nuclear weapons he dealt with ranged from their design and efficiency to defensive steps against them. He also played a significant role in developing certain advanced missile warheads and in devising ways to detect underground nuclear tests.<ref name=NYTimes/>}}

Albert Latter's brother [[Richard Latter]] (1923–1999) was also a noteworthy physicist and they worked together at RAND.<ref name=PT2000>{{cite journal|author=Brode, Harold L.|title=Obituary. Richard Latter|journal=Physics Today|volume=53|issue=4|pages=83–84|year=2000|doi=10.1063/1.883065|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 1971 Albert Latter resigned from RAND<ref name=NYTimes/> and, together his brother Richard and most of RAND's physics department,<ref name=PT2000/> founded in [[Marina del Rey]] the defense research company R&D Associates (RDA) which was acquired in 1983 by Logicon Inc.,<ref name=NYTimes/> which became a subsidiary of [[Northrop Grumman]] in 1997.<ref>{{cite news|title=Northrop Agrees to Buy Logicon for $750 Million|date=May 6, 1997|newspaper=L. A. Times|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-05-06-fi-56066-story.html}}</ref> Albert Latter was the president and [[Chief executive officer|CEO]] of R&D Associates until his retirement in 1985.<ref name=LATimes/>

He received the 1964 [[Ernest O. Lawrence Award]] from the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]] "for contributions in the determination of the destructive effects as well as in the decoupling of nuclear explosions and in the design of nuclear weapons."<ref>{{cite book|chapter=E. O. Lawrence Award|title=Annual Report to Congress of the Atomic Energy Commission|date=January 1965|location=Washington, D.C.|publisher=United States Government Printing Office|page=33|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Jj_VAAAAMAAJ&pg=RA1-PA33}}</ref>

Upon his death Albert Latter was survived by his wife, two daughter, and three grandchildren.<ref name=NYTimes/>
